questions.question: Ciprofloxacin. Describe an associated effect with each organ system
questions.model_answer: Cardiovascular: QTc prolongation (risk of torsades de pointes). Endocrine: dysglycemia (both hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia, particularly in diabetics). Musculoskeletal: tendinopathy/tendon rupture (especially Achilles tendon) and arthropathy/cartilage damage. Nervous system: CNS toxicity - lowered seizure threshold, peripheral neuropathy, and psychiatric effects (confusion, agitation, insomnia).

questions.question: Post-antibiotic effect

parts.text: Name two classes of antibiotics which exhibit this phenomenon.

cohort_answer.text: PAE = inhibition of bacterial growth following exposure to an antibiotic even after drug concentration falls below MIC, exhibited by delay before microorganisms re-enter log-growth in vitro. Possible mechanisms: nonlethal damage induced by the antimicrobial resulting in slow recovery; persistence of antimicrobial at bacterial binding sites (ribosomes, DNA gyrase) and periplasmic space. Specific microorganism-antimicrobial combination is most important factor influencing presence/duration of PAE, along with concentration and length of exposure. In human studies, aminoglycosides (extended PAE against GNB) effective with once-daily dosing. Classes exhibiting PAE: Aminoglycosides (PAE against GNB, lasts 2-6 hrs); Fluoroquinolones (PAE against GNB, lasts 2-6 hrs); beta-lactams generally do not exhibit PAE against GNB (except imipenem) but induce ~2hr PAE against GP organisms.

questions.question: Ciprofloxacin

cohort_answer.text: Cardiovascular: QTc prolongation. Endocrine: Dysglycemia (both hyper and hypo). MSK: Connective tissue toxicity, particularly acute tendinitis and increased risk of aortic dissection. Neurologic: Peripheral neuropathy - may be irreversible; CNS: neuropsych up to toxic psychosis, can cause seizures

questions.question: Regarding fluoroquinolones:

parts.text: What is the mechanism of action?
What is the concern with using fluoroquinolones in pregnancy?
List SIX acute and possibly life-threatening adverse effects.

questions.model_answer:
a) Mechanism of action: fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II, predominant target in gram-negatives) and topoisomerase IV (predominant target in gram-positives), enzymes required for DNA supercoiling, replication, and repair, leading to bacterial DNA damage and cell death.
b) Concern in pregnancy: animal studies have shown fluoroquinolone-associated arthropathy/cartilage damage in immature weight-bearing joints; although human data are less conclusive, fluoroquinolones are generally avoided in pregnancy due to this theoretical risk of fetal cartilage/joint toxicity.
c) 6 acute/life-threatening adverse effects: (1) QTc prolongation and torsades de pointes; (2) tendon rupture (especially Achilles); (3) aortic aneurysm or dissection; (4) seizures/CNS toxicity; (5) severe hypoglycemia; (6) severe hypersensitivity reactions (anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis).

questions.question: For the following phrases, please fill with one of the choices from the list provided so that the phrase becomes true. Choices: Acyclovir over valacyclovir; Valganciclovir over valacyclovir; Famciclovir over acyclovir; Atovaquone over dapsone; Doxycycline over TMP-SMX; Fluconazole over caspofungin; Liposomal amphotericin B over amphotericin deoxycholate; Piperacillin-tazobactam over meropenem; Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin; Metronidazole over clindamycin; Azithromycin over clarithromycin; Ampicillin over cloxacillin; Cefazolin over cloxacillin.

parts.text: I chose ____ because it offers better renal penetration.
I chose ____ because of the antibiotics not used to treat C. difficile, it has not been associated with an increased risk of CDI.
I chose ____ because it has more CMV activity.
I chose ____ because my patient is taking carbamazepine.
I chose ___ because I needed an agent to cover bacterial infection of the CNS.
I chose ____ because my patient has G6PD deficiency.

cohort_answer.text:
Acyclovir over valacyclovir: HSV meningitis/encephalitis.
Valganciclovir over valacyclovir: Herpes B treatment better activity, CMV treatment.
Famciclovir over acyclovir: Uncomplicated zoster (famciclovir higher oral bioavailability than acyclovir, dosed TID rather than 5 times daily).
Atovaquone over dapsone: G6PD deficiency, Toxoplasmosis.
Doxycycline over TMP-SMX: Someone on Ramipril and Spironolactone with MRSA infection may want Doxycycline over TMP/SMX given risk of hyperkalemia.
Fluconazole over caspofungin: Cryptococcus not covered by echinocandins, urinary or CNS infections.
Liposomal amphotericin B over amphotericin deoxycholate: CNS infections, disseminated histoplasmosis, suspected mucormycosis.
Piperacillin-tazobactam over meropenem: Enterococcus.
Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin: Anaerobic activity is best with moxi.
Metronidazole over clindamycin: Bacteroides fragilis, increasing clinda resistance.
Azithromycin over clarithromycin: Better for gram-negatives, esp. M catarrhalis and H flu.
Ampicillin over cloxacillin: Enterococci, Listeria.
Cefazolin over cloxacillin: Surgical prophylaxis, penicillin allergy, AIN, heart failure.

parts.text: I would pick _____ over _____ because patient on carbamazepine
I would pick _____ over _____ because patient has G6PD deficiency
I would pick _____ over _____ because drug NOT used for C.diff treatment and NOT associated with development of C.diff
I would pick _____ over _____ because it has superior renal penetration
I would pick _____ over _____ because it works better for CMV
I would pick _____ over _____ because I need CNS coverage

questions.model_answer:
a) Because patient is on carbamazepine (a potent CYP3A4 inducer with significant drug-interaction potential with azoles): choose caspofungin over fluconazole to avoid a clinically significant CYP-mediated interaction.
b) Because patient has G6PD deficiency: choose atovaquone over dapsone (dapsone causes oxidative hemolysis in G6PD deficiency; atovaquone does not).
c) Because the drug is NOT used for C. difficile treatment and NOT associated with causing C. difficile: choose doxycycline over Septra (TMP-SMX) - doxycycline carries a low risk of precipitating C. difficile infection and is not a CDI treatment.
d) Because of superior renal/urinary penetration: choose cefazolin over cloxacillin (cefazolin achieves higher urinary concentrations; cloxacillin has substantial hepatobiliary elimination).
e) Because it works better for CMV: choose valganciclovir over acyclovir (acyclovir has minimal activity against CMV; valganciclovir/ganciclovir are the drugs of choice).
f) Because CNS coverage is needed: choose moxifloxacin over levofloxacin (moxifloxacin achieves higher CNS penetration due to greater lipophilicity).

questions.question: Describe the specific mechanisms of actions for the following anti-tubercular medications.
questions.model_answer: Isoniazid: a prodrug activated by mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase (KatG); the activated form inhibits InhA, blocking mycolic acid synthesis and disrupting the mycobacterial cell wall. Rifamycins: inhibit the beta-subunit of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (rpoB), blocking bacterial RNA transcription. Linezolid: binds the 23S rRNA of the 50S ribosomal subunit, preventing formation of the 70S initiation complex and inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis. Levofloxacin: inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, preventing DNA supercoiling/replication. Bedaquiline: inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase, depleting intracellular ATP and producing bactericidal activity over several days.

questions.question: Interactions of tacrolimus with: Ciprofloxacin, Voriconazole, Rifampin, Clarithromycin.

parts.text: Describe the interaction of tacrolimus (a CYP3A4 substrate) with each of the listed drugs.

cohort_answer.text: Tacrolimus is a CYP3A4 substrate. Ciprofloxacin - weakly inhibits CYP3A4, may increase tacrolimus. Voriconazole - inhibits CYP3A4, increases tacrolimus. Rifampin - induces CYP3A4, decreases tacrolimus levels (strongest contraindication; rifabutin should be used instead of rifampin to avoid interaction and reduce risk of acute graft rejection). Clarithromycin (and other macrolides) - inhibits CYP3A4, increases tacrolimus.

parts.text: Why do you need to test for G6PD in P. vivax infection?
Describe the two proposed mechanisms of glucose metabolism alteration with fluoroquinolone antibiotics

cohort_answer.text: In P. vivax and P. ovale, the dormant hypnozoite liver stage needs to be eradicated; the 2 antimalarials with activity against hypnozoites are primaquine and tafenoquine, both of which can cause hemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency. FQ glucose mechanisms: stimulate release of insulin; interaction with hyperglycemic agents (e.g. glyburide).

questions.question: Describe the mechanism of: Rifampin, Isoniazid, Linezolid, Moxifloxacin, Bedaquiline.

cohort_answer.text: Rifampin: Inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, occurring as a result of drug binding in the polymerase subunit deep within the DNA/RNA channel, facilitating direct blocking of elongating RNA. Isoniazid: Inhibits mycolic acid synthesis, interfering with cell wall synthesis, producing a bactericidal effect; also disrupts DNA, lipid, carbohydrate, and NAD synthesis/metabolism. Linezolid: Inhibits initiation of bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 23S rRNA component of the 50S ribosome (contains 5S rRNA, 23S rRNA, 34 proteins); also suppresses production of bacterial toxins such as Panton-Valentine leukocidin, alpha-hemolysin, and TSST-1. Moxifloxacin: Directly inhibits DNA synthesis; binds to DNA gyrase and DNA topoisomerase IV, generating DNA cleavage. Bedaquiline: Inhibits bacterial ATP synthase; ATP production is required for cellular energy production and its loss leads to inhibition of mycobacterial growth within hours
